DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
This review finds that the case for a weekend rate rise is plausible: you're well below your competitive set, and there's room before revenue falls. But four problems undermine the paper as written:

1. **The revenue figure uses the wrong room count.** Section 2 says Harbourside has **112 rooms**; Section 5 calculates on **124**. With 112 rooms the same formula gives about **£184,000**, not £204,000.
2. **The price-sensitivity "test" is confounded by seasonality.** The June→July rise from 81% to 89% coincides with the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, which Section 2 itself names as the reasons July and August are strongest. It tells you nothing about how guests respond to price.
3. **£204,000 is a ceiling, not a floor.** It assumes every weekend room is sold at BAR and that occupancy doesn't move at all. Wedding blocks, group and corporate rates, and OTA commission all reduce it, and zero occupancy loss is an optimistic assumption, not a prudent one.
4. **The two-night minimum collides with the wedding business.** Weddings make up about 38% of Saturday bookings, and those guests typically stay one night (Saturday to Sunday). The paper doesn't say whether they're exempt. If they aren't, you risk losing them. If they are, the minimum applies to far fewer guests than implied.

## 1. Room count: 112 or 124?

| Basis | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Paper (124 rooms) | 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£203,758** ✓ |
| Section 2 (112 rooms) | 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 | **£184,038** |

The rest of the formula checks out:
- 104 weekend nights = 52 Fridays + 52 Saturdays ✓.
- The 2025 average occupancy from Table 1 is 79.2% ✓.

But the hotel is described as 112 rooms, so unless that's wrong, the headline figure is about £20,000 too high before any other adjustment.

## 2. The June→July test doesn't measure price sensitivity

- The rate rose in the **last week of June**. July occupancy rose to 89%.
- But Section 2 says July and August are the strongest months *because of* the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy would almost certainly have risen anyway.
- June (81%) was actually **below** May (85%) before the increase, so the jump says even less about the rate.

**A more useful test:** compare July–December 2025 against **July–December 2024**, the same months a year earlier. That shows whether occupancy held up against the previous year after the £10 rise. If you have it, look at booking pace (pick-up) in the weeks after the change against the same weeks of 2024.

Also note:
- The £10 rise was **+7.4%**. The proposed £20 is **+13.8%**, so even a clean result from last year would only partly carry over.
- The 8.4 value-for-money score was earned at £135–£145. At £165 you'd **match the cheapest competitor** rather than undercutting it, so the score may not hold.

## 3. Why £204,000 is a ceiling, not a floor

The cover note says the estimate is "deliberately conservative." In fact it assumes the most favourable conditions:

**Not every room is sold at BAR**
- Wedding blocks are about 38% of Saturday bookings, typically at group rates.
- Contracted corporate and group rates are honoured (Section 6).
- Packages and other discounted channels are also usually priced off BAR rather than at it.
- The paper should state what share of weekend room nights is actually sold at BAR, and apply the £20 only to that share. *For illustration only:* if 60% of weekend nights were at BAR, the gain would be about £110,000 on 112 rooms.

**OTA commission**
- If a significant share of BAR bookings come through online travel agents, the hotel keeps only the net of commission on each extra £20.

**Zero price elasticity**
- Assuming occupancy is "maintained at 2025 levels" means assuming no guest is put off by a 14% rise. That's the optimistic end of the range, not the prudent end.

**The two-night minimum isn't free upside**
- On Saturdays that wouldn't have sold out, a minimum stay turns away one-night guests, and some of those rooms will stay empty. It can reduce revenue as well as add to it.

**Partial first year**
- Bookings already taken before 15 May for June onwards are at £145, so year-one uplift will be lower.

## 4. The two-night minimum and weddings

This is the biggest operational gap:
- About **38% of Saturday room bookings** are wedding guests from Quayside Hall.
- They "arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning," a classic one-night stay.
- A two-night minimum on stays including Saturday applies directly to them.

The paper doesn't say which of two outcomes follows:
1. **Wedding blocks are exempt.** Then the minimum mostly affects the remaining 62% of Saturday guests, and the case for it is narrower. Say so explicitly.
2. **Wedding blocks are not exempt.** Then wedding guests may book elsewhere, which risks the relationship with the venue next door.

**Also worth considering:**
- Apply the minimum only on **high-demand Saturdays**. You sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. That's standard practice, and it avoids turning away guests on quieter weekends.
- Quantify current single-night Saturday stays, excluding weddings, so the "further revenue" claim has some basis.

## 5. Monitoring

The five-point trigger is reasonable, and there's useful context the paper could add:

**Break-even occupancy.** At £145 and 79% occupancy, revenue per available weekend room is £114.55. At £165, the same revenue needs occupancy of **69.4%**. So, *for BAR rooms*, occupancy could fall about 9–10 points before the rate rise loses money. That's actually a strong argument for the proposal, and the paper doesn't make it.

**Improvements to the monitoring:**
- Monitor **RevPAR or room revenue** alongside occupancy, since occupancy alone doesn't show whether the trade-off is working.
- Track wedding and group pick-up separately, to catch any effect of the minimum stay.
- A monthly report means up to a month of losses before review. Since pick-up is reviewed weekly anyway, let the trigger work on weekly pace against 2025.

## 6. What holds up

- **Competitor positioning:** £145 is genuinely £20–£35 below the set (£165–£180), and £165 sits at the bottom of that range. A rise is reasonable.
- **The occupancy table** and the **79% average** are correct.
- **Saturday constraint:** 31 sell-outs is a real signal of pricing power on peak dates.
- **The value-for-money score** is a genuine strength, so long as it isn't over-claimed as proof that guests aren't sensitive to price.
- **Implementation:** two weeks' OTA notice, honouring contracted rates, and weekly pick-up review are all good practice.

## Suggested changes before approval

1. Confirm the room count and restate revenue (about £184,000 on 112 rooms) as a maximum.
2. Apply the £20 only to the BAR share of weekend room nights, net of OTA commission.
3. Replace the June→July evidence with a year-on-year comparison (2025 vs 2024).
4. Add the break-even occupancy (about 69%) as the main risk measure, and monitor RevPAR.
5. State how wedding blocks are treated under the minimum stay, and consider applying the minimum only on high-demand Saturdays.
6. Present a range (low, central, high) rather than a single "at least" figure.

The proposal may well be right: the rate looks low against your competitive set, and the break-even maths gives a good cushion. It will be far more persuasive presented with a realistic range than with an overstated "at least £204,000."
